## 0.6.1 (2026-10-13)


### 🚀 LoopTroop — What's New Since v0.6.0

A big round of bug fixes, stability improvements, and quality-of-life updates!

1. 🛑 **Stop & Retry AI Models** — Stop or restart slow, stuck, or blocked models individually during multi-model council rounds, without restarting everyone else.
2. 🔍 **Better Error Pages** — More detailed errors showing what went wrong, which model failed, and useful debugging information.
3. 🔄 **Smoother Error Recovery** — Fix an issue, retry or continue, and return to your workflow without getting stuck on the error screen.
4. 🛠️ **More Reliable OpenCode Startup** — Fixed startup failures, port conflicts, and process management issues.
5. 🤖 **Improved Model Detection** — More reliable model loading, refreshing, and provider detection.
6. 🐛 **Fewer Unexpected Failures** — Fixed OpenCode v2 issues that could incorrectly block or interrupt workflows.
7. 🧠 **Smarter AI Response Handling** — Better handling of incorrectly formatted model responses, reducing unnecessary failures.
8. ⏭️ **Skip All AI Questions** — Skip multiple pending questions across different models in one click, with improved timeout settings.
9. 💻 **Better Windows & Linux Support** — Fixed installation, compatibility, and reliability issues across platforms.
10. ⚡ **Up to 20× Faster CLI** — Much faster commands, a smaller package, and lighter builds. [#259](https://github.com/looptroop-ai/LoopTroop/pull/259)

**✨ Overall:** Faster, more stable, easier to recover from errors, and more control over your AI models!

### Summary

- You can stop or retry one council model while the others keep drafting or voting, instead of waiting for a slow model's timeout.
- Error page recovery actions (Retry, Continue, Retry with extra note, Edit setup plan, and Cancel) automatically return the workspace to the resumed workflow status or canceled view and clear active error selection.
- OpenCode v2 scans and prompts tolerate private bookkeeping events safely and avoid automatic title calls that can block a finished response; OpenCode v1 remains supported.
- Ticket errors name failed readiness checks and show the five newest debug records, each collapsed in Technical details; live and saved debug logs redact credentials in every phase.
- OpenCode communication errors explain the failed operation and available cause, and coverage logs distinguish checks, response attempts, and reconnections.
- Interview batches recover safely when a model mixes field tags with YAML, preserving question text and recording the corrections in the ticket log.
- AI question actions stay visible, with a Skip all option for questions across every model tab.
- Development dependency updates fix command injection and denial-of-service vulnerabilities.
- AI question settings share Advanced rows across Configuration, Project, and New Ticket, with a nested wait that preserves edits and prevents invalid saves or starts.
- LoopTroop prefers configured and home OpenCode installations over PATH and reports which executable it selected.
- OpenCode v2 model discovery waits for providers; Configuration keeps model lists live, refreshes slow discovery, shows model counts, and collapses providers in the results.
- Published-install checks avoid Windows installer and startup hangs, keep PowerShell modules and OpenCode probes working, and apply CI repairs to existing releases.
- Windows PowerShell commands and installers load their standard modules when launched from PowerShell 7 through LoopTroop.
- Release publication waits for npm's package scans, includes the executable resolver needed to publish container tags, and reads npm metadata correctly during recovery and channel repair.
- LoopTroop starts OpenCode from `~/.opencode/bin` again on Ubuntu, Fedora and other Linux desktops, where the OpenCode installer creates that folder group-writable.
- When another server already holds OpenCode's default port, LoopTroop starts its own OpenCode on the next free port and tells you where it went.
- `looptroop doctor` compares your Node with the newest release of your own Node line, says what `gh` is still needed for, and names the checks that actually stop LoopTroop from running.
- `looptroop` commands such as `status` and `--help` answer in about a third of a second instead of several seconds, and LoopTroop installs about 30 MB less.
- Token counts shown in the interface are now a quick estimate of four characters per token.

### Added

- Added README badges for the latest release, MIT license, published package's Node requirement, OpenSSF Scorecard, total downloads, CI status, and test coverage. The download badge uses the installation page's existing statistics API and links to its source breakdown and history; CI and coverage badges report the main branch.
- Added **Stop** and **Retry** for a single council model in Council Drafting Questions, Voting on Questions, Council Drafting Specs, Voting on Specs, Council Drafting Blueprint, and Voting on Blueprint. During drafting they are small buttons in the top-right corner of the window a model's chip opens; during voting they are icons on each voter's badge in the Voter Status row of Voting Details. Both always ask for confirmation.
  - Stop closes that model's OpenCode session and the step continues with the others. The model shows as **Stopped**, keeps nothing it wrote, and does not count toward Min Council Quorum. When the stop leaves too few models to reach the quorum, the confirmation says the step will fail; you can still go ahead. If it was the last model working, the step moves on right away. A stop lasts for that step only, so the model still votes in the next one.
  - Retry restarts that one model with a full AI response timeout of its own, so the step can run longer than usual. It is offered while at least one model is still working: on a model still working, on one that ended without a usable result, and on one that finished fine, whose draft or vote is then thrown away for good.
  - In Council Drafting Specs, Retry from the Part 1 chip redoes Full Answers and the PRD draft; Retry from the Part 2 chip keeps Full Answers that passed validation and redoes only the PRD draft. Stopping a model there throws away both parts, so nothing it wrote reaches the vote or the refinement.
  - In Council Drafting Specs and Council Drafting Blueprint, a model waiting on an AI question has that question closed as soon as you confirm, recorded in the skip trail as refused by you with the new expiry reason `member_stopped` or `member_restarted`. That holds even when OpenCode never confirms the stop, so the question no longer holds every model's clock still, and it does not come back later, after a restart included. Each stop and retry is written to the phase log.
  - New endpoints `POST /api/tickets/:id/council/members/stop` and `/retry`. A second action on the same model while the first is under way is refused with `MEMBER_BUSY`, and `part` is only accepted for Council Drafting Specs.
  - Retry from Blocked Error after a council step first confirms that the step's leftover OpenCode sessions are stopped, and answers `409` until they are, so the retried round cannot reconnect to a model whose stop never confirmed.
- Added **Skip all** when more than one AI question is pending. It skips every request pending when confirmed, across all model tabs, including questions that arrive while you enter the optional reason. The same reason is recorded for each request; each rejection can succeed or fail independently. Bulk confirmation is disabled while any answer or skip is being submitted, and Back remains available.

### Changed

- Interview, PRD, and beads coverage logs separate phase preparation from model work, identify each coverage check and response attempt, and say when they reconnect to an existing session. PRD and beads logs also identify candidate versions, audit results, and gap-resolution revisions. Requested approval-screen gap fixes use a separate manual coverage fix number and show their check count without an automatic-limit denominator. Reconnecting keeps the same check or fix number; retry limits and coverage budgets are unchanged.
- Reorganized the error panel around one failed-phase heading, the full error message, and any distinct underlying cause. Removed repeated active-error labels and generic failure advice while preserving explanations for recognized failures. Live recovery guidance names only available actions, recovery buttons come before Cancel, and paused-bead context appears before technical details. A paused current bead takes precedence over an older failed bead's notes. Historical errors show their own message and phase without current bead counters or notes. Technical details is collapsed by default and closes again when selecting another ticket or occurrence, while background refreshes of the same failure preserve its open state and keyboard focus. Expanding it shows captured model, session, provider, timing, token counts including cache reads/writes, and a bounded provider response preview when available. The preview preserves structured formatting and repeated lines and supports keyboard scrolling. The error stays visible when details are closed, and duplicate provider-message rows are omitted.
- New OpenCode v2 sessions use the title "LoopTroop" to avoid the separate model call for automatic session naming. LoopTroop ticket titles and OpenCode v1 session creation are unchanged.
- Moved AI questions and AI question wait into Configuration **Advanced**. Across Configuration, Project, New Ticket, and saved drafts, the wait is an indented subitem directly below AI questions, without a separator. Configuration offers **Default / Custom**: **Default** uses 5 minutes, and **Custom** accepts whole minutes from 1 to 60. Project and Ticket retain **Inherit / Custom**, showing the effective duration and its source. Selecting **Default** or **Inherit** resets the custom override and replaces the separate Clear override action. Configuration treats a mode change as an unsaved edit even when both modes use 5 minutes.
- Saved drafts save valid custom wait input when you leave the field, press Enter, or close the view. Mode changes still save immediately. Further setting changes, description saves, and Start wait for earlier saves to succeed. A failed save cancels queued actions and shows an error. Controls keep keyboard focus during saves and lock during Start or while inherited settings load.
- Model picker provider headings now collapse or expand their own models in place. The separate provider-button panel above the results is removed; collapsed headings stay visible. Starting a search expands provider groups; later collapses hide their models, and keyboard selection skips those hidden models.
- OpenCode resolution searches `LOOPTROOP_TRUSTED_EXECUTABLE_DIRS` first, then the first absolute directory from `OPENCODE_INSTALL_DIR` or `OPENCODE_DIR`, then `~/.opencode/bin`, then Windows system directories and ordinary `PATH`. Canonical PATH aliases keep their invocation spelling within that order. These directory settings come from LoopTroop's environment; project PATH additions cannot override them. Missing executables fall through to the next directory, while a trust refusal stops resolution. Use the operator override to choose another installation deliberately.
- `looptroop doctor` keeps marking a missing `gh` with `✗`, but adds that LoopTroop starts without it and that a ticket needs it before coding starts, when its pre-flight check runs. Its last line names the checks that stop LoopTroop from running, for example `LoopTroop cannot run until this is fixed: opencode.`, instead of pointing at every `✗` above it.
- When OpenCode's default address (`127.0.0.1:4096`) is held by a server LoopTroop cannot use, because it rejects LoopTroop's password or is not OpenCode, LoopTroop leaves that server alone and starts its own OpenCode on the next free port. OpenCode v2 makes up a new password for every `opencode serve` started by hand, and other tools built on OpenCode take 4096 too, so a server left running there used to stop LoopTroop from starting at all. A server that answers with a 5xx error still counts as an OpenCode that is starting up: LoopTroop waits for it, then judges it by what it answers once it is up. An address you set with `LOOPTROOP_OPENCODE_BASE_URL` or `opencodeBaseUrl` is never moved, and the move never takes LoopTroop's own web port. When LoopTroop's own address is the one OpenCode would use, as with `looptroop start --port 4096`, the default address moves too and `doctor` names the port it would take; an address you set on that port and host stops the start, even when a server already answers there, with a message that names both settings. `looptroop start`, `looptroop open`, `looptroop status`, `looptroop doctor` and the daemon log say where OpenCode went and why. Before the first start, `doctor` reports a held default port as a warning that names the port a start would take, and as a failure when no port is free.
- Token counts are now estimated at four characters per token, shown as `~N Tokens (estimate)` in artifact Raw panes and bead Input and Output, and as `~N tokens` on the relevant-files scan card. The prompt context budget uses the same estimate. The old count was exact only for GPT-5's tokenizer, so it was already an estimate for every other model. The estimate is close for English prose and code, and counts only a third to a half of the real tokens for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean text. Because trimming uses it, mostly Chinese, Japanese, or Korean context can reach the 100,000-token budget while holding more than 100,000 real tokens.

### Performance

- `looptroop` commands load only the code they run. The CLI is now built as a small entry plus shared files under `dist/server/chunks/`, so `looptroop --version`, `status`, and `--help` no longer load the database layer and every other dependency before doing anything. On the machine this was measured on they went from about 5 seconds to about 0.35 seconds. The daemon and the package entry stay single self-contained files, so a daemon still running during an upgrade keeps working until you restart it.
- The npm package shrank from 4.4 MB to 2.8 MB (16.6 MB to 11.3 MB unpacked). The CLI no longer carries its own full copy of the server, and the web interface no longer ships a tokenizer.
- Removed the `gpt-tokenizer` dependency: 27 MB and 1,537 files on every install, a 2 MB download in the web interface, and almost a second of load time for every command.

### Security

- Provider diagnostics remove terminal control sequences before redacting recognized credential fields and common credential formats, then apply the preview length limit. This prevents control sequences or truncation from exposing credentials in error details. Redaction covers camelCase credential keys, credential assignments split across lines in formatted JSON, labeled authorization values, Basic and Bearer credentials, complete cookie header values, and URL credentials, queries, and fragments, while common failure prose remains readable. Repeated unterminated terminal sequences no longer cause slow diagnostic processing. All phase Debug records, including readiness probes, coding and council sessions, redact credentials before serialization, live-stream truncation, broadcast or storage. Readiness stream events also protect diagnostic copies outside the Debug view. Model, session, process, timing and numeric token metadata remain available. Security regressions inspect complete raw stored logs through the existing protected file reader and construct synthetic password examples at runtime, preserving their checks without misleading alerts about fixture paths or hard-coded credentials.
- Updated development dependencies to patched releases of `shell-quote`, `brace-expansion` and `source-map-js`. Their fixes prevent command injection when quoting tokens after shell comments and denial of service when expanding nested braces or reading malformed indexed source maps.

### Removed

- Local OpenCode configuration and plugins in `.opencode/` are now ignored by Git. The repository no longer includes the listener-limit plugin.

### Fixed

- Running the CLI file directly (`node dist/server/cli/cli.js start` rather than the installed `looptroop` command) no longer starts the daemon twice in one process. The second start failed against the first one's lock and wrote `LoopTroop is already running` with the daemon's own pid to the log.
- An AI question could be closed twice when its session ended while its own wait was running out. That wrote two skip records and let every model's clock run again while another question was still waiting.
- Answering or skipping an AI question that was closed in the meantime (its session ended, or its model was stopped) answers `409` instead of reporting success and logging an answer that was never recorded.
- When a session with several open AI questions ends, every skip record names the same related questions; the last one used to name none.
- A PRD drafting model whose step failed, because its structured retries or its time ran out, now has its OpenCode session stopped. It used to stay open.
- In Council Drafting Specs, a model whose OpenCode prompt never answers, not even after its time ran out, now times out as in the other council steps. The step used to wait for it indefinitely, with no error.
- The Council Drafting Questions details no longer say LoopTroop stops the round early when too many drafts fail. The quorum is checked once every model has finished.
- After Retry, Continue, Retry with extra note, Edit setup plan, or non-deleting Cancel on an error page, the workspace follows the ticket to its resumed status (or Canceled view) instead of staying on the resolved error. Error selection is cleared when leaving BLOCKED_ERROR without disrupting historical error reviews during other workflow transitions.
- Every ticket error includes its phase, occurrence, timestamp, full sanitized error, and the last five matching Debug-view records in Technical details, even when no model or provider metadata was recorded. The records appear newest first and each starts collapsed. Expanding a record shows its complete structured data after credential redaction; the section also stays collapsed by default. Recorded errors use the failed phase's time window so later retries, including reused OpenCode sessions, cannot replace the evidence. Missing metadata or logs and failed log reads are explicit, and the separate phase log still provides the full history. Error type and a bounded sanitized stack are retained when available. Checking Readiness errors name every failed doctor check in the original error and raw evidence, use regular text for the step prefix and bold only the actionable cause, and preserve capability-probe model, provider, exact session, failed operation, and original cause. A reported expired provider login explains why the actual model request failed even when OpenCode health and model discovery passed. Server health, model listing and session creation authentication failures stay attributed to OpenCode, and generic access denials do not suggest refreshing provider credentials. Workspace initialization failures retain the actual error and cause stacks with the initialization operation and existing INIT codes, keeping Git authentication separate from AI-provider login advice.
- Failure evidence includes native OpenCode records using either timestamp format. Errors without a saved occurrence apply their time bounds on the server before selecting five records, so newer activity cannot hide the failure. Redaction applies to evidence entries while preserving ordinary log pages, exports, and opaque cursor metadata; the added native raw-line field is sanitized for every reader. Doctor reports are sanitized before logging or artifact storage, and compact failed-check summaries avoid copying detailed evidence and repeated stacks into ticket payloads. Every failure line keeps its step and error-type prefixes and HTTP status in regular text; only the actionable cause is bold. Provider-login guidance requires provider evidence, so expired-token messages from tests and setup commands keep their own phase's explanation. Existing preserved sessions can Continue following a known OpenCode-server HTTP 401 or 403 rejection once server login or access is repaired and the usual exact-session safety checks pass. Failed session creation without a session stays Retry-only, and model-provider authentication failures remain ineligible for Continue. PRD editor regression tests check independent story and epic actions within separate test budgets without increasing timeouts. Provider rejections at prompt dispatch retain their provider identity, status, error type, and response preview, including structured model-step failures, rather than inheriting server-login recovery. Ambiguous prompt errors reporting only Unauthorized or Forbidden without explicit server or provider evidence keep captured metadata with neutral guidance and Retry, without assumed provider identity, login-refresh advice, or Continue. Known server login and permission failures can still Continue after repair with an existing owned session; billing, quota, invalid-request, and policy denials do not qualify for that exception. Repeated session-error records remain separate evidence. Cookie redaction keeps unambiguous neighboring diagnostic fields and valid expanded JSON, and initialization error messages are sanitized before events, logs, stored errors, or API responses. Explicit billing or payment-method evidence in a provider 401 suppresses misleading login-refresh advice while retaining the reported type, status, and response preview; the 401 stays Retry-only and existing provider 402 continuation is unchanged. Long whitespace or escape sequences in malformed errors no longer cause repeated scans during URL redaction or headline formatting, keeping error processing responsive. Native session ownership is discovered before filtering record times, so matching native failures stay visible when ownership was recorded before the failure window; ticket, phase, attempt, and bead scope still exclude unrelated evidence. Aborts and timeouts retain their existing handling; other HTTP failure-body read errors preserve the known status, any established origin, and original read cause when available. An unreadable 404 does not prove an existing session is gone or cause its ownership to be abandoned. Unidentified prompt rejections retain neutral guidance and Retry.
- OpenCode communication failures preserve the original error cause instead of reducing it to `fetch failed`, including exhausted session-creation retries and nested AI retry errors. Error messages name the failed operation and reported error, then point to captured connection details or say when no exact connection cause was reported. Collapsed Technical details includes the operation and available bounded, sanitized connection diagnostics without guessing a timeout or model rejection. Non-connection codes stay separate from Connection code, and terminal session failures retain their known operation.
- Interview batch parsing repairs known field-tag formatting only after all ordinary parsing candidates fail. The repair requires an explicit `INTERVIEW_BATCH` wrapper and all five known root fields, converts existing scalar values and YAML containers, and corrects the observed stray terminal questions closer while preserving literal XML inside question text. Existing validation and normalization still apply. Ambiguous, conflicting, truncated, or unknown structures are rejected without inventing content, including conflicting question and option aliases. Rejected field-tag repairs name the structural problem in retry and error messages. Shortened fallbacks from the same tagged batch cannot discard its emitted final-batch flag or commentary, including when tags are indented; a malformed earlier wrapper cannot swallow later independent output. Complete ordinary candidates keep their existing priority. Malformed field tags with long whitespace no longer cause excessive backtracking during guard checks. Accepted correction notices name the repair rule and affected fields; short before/after excerpts remain in structured log-entry data. Successful structured retries are also recorded. Other parsers retain their existing repair rules.
- Initial interview-batch failures that block the ticket retain the model, exact OpenCode session, and available finish and token/cache metrics in blocked-error diagnostics. A cleanup failure preserves the original failure as its cause, and a confirmed stopped session is not aborted again if starting its replacement fails.
- Interview coverage timeouts retain the model, session, operation, and diagnostic codes in the blocked error for existing recovery checks. Coverage summaries recognize the saved PRD revision version rather than reporting its previous candidate.
- Fixed valid OpenCode v2 prompts failing when private title or compaction events leave gaps in the public stream. A new connection must account for its first event before later private gaps can be accepted. Malformed events clearly belonging to other sessions no longer block the ticket, while missing or conflicting routing still stops unsafe responses. Late events inside an earlier gap and log watermarks behind an observed event are rejected. Reconnects still verify the full missing history, retry transient connection failures, and preserve mapping state across failed replay attempts without submitting the prompt again. Complete, valid replay that proves new progress resets the retry budget; empty reconnects remain bounded. Replaced and failed connections are released after cleanup finishes, so long prompts do not retain every earlier connection and cancellation still waits for cleanup.
- Pre-flight checks, execution setup, bead failures, and final tests keep their actual failure text in the ticket and error history instead of hiding it behind a generic label or diagnostic code. Coding failures put the final stopping reason first, followed by attempts from newest to oldest, so short ticket summaries name the reason the bead stopped.
- Reused repeated transport and ticket-error test setup while retaining the same scenarios and assertions. Iterator and path expressions keep their existing behavior while giving static analysis clearer inputs.
- AI question confirmations clear when their requests resolve, when you go Back, or when you collapse the panel. Bulk reasons survive model-tab changes, and every failed rejection is shown for retry. Rapid clicks cannot send duplicate answers or skips, and a double-click on **Skip all** cannot confirm it. Confirmation labels distinguish the selected request from all pending questions; **Send answers** submits only the selected model's batch. Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends an answer or confirms a skip from its text field. On very short viewports, the whole panel scrolls so its fields remain reachable.
- AI question panels keep answer and skip buttons beside the waiting count in a fixed header. Only the question content scrolls, and the panel can use up to half the viewport so ordinary questions have room to fit. Long words and URLs wrap within the panel.
- Artifact compare-and-set tests now run in isolated integration workers, matching their use of real Git worktrees and SQLite databases.
- Aligned AI-question controls to the right and added contextual `?` help links for both options. Wait controls are disabled when effective AI questions are **Off**, including when **Inherit** resolves to **Off**. Turning questions off shows the last valid duration and preserves the chosen mode and unfinished input. Inactive wait errors do not block saving. Turning questions back on restores the input and its validation.
- Collapsing **Advanced** preserves unfinished wait input and validation. An invalid active custom wait blocks Configuration and Project saves, ticket creation, and Start; closing an edited form asks before discarding it. Validation and draft save errors remain visible while Advanced is closed. AI question selectors use one Tab stop per group and support arrow keys. Wait values use whole minutes in both the controls and API. The Custom input keeps unfinished edits during background updates and stays synchronized after React interrupts and retries a render.
- Configuration waits for the saved profile before enabling edits, preventing late loading from replacing saved settings with defaults. Project creation checks repository validation on every submit, including Enter. Closing New Ticket restores keyboard focus to its opener.
- Editing or removing a council member in Configuration preserves each remaining model picker's state, including empty rows.
- Log following compares exact file identities, fixing skipped replacement bytes when large file IDs rounded to the same number during rename-and-create rotation.
- Closed model pickers expose `aria-busy` during manual refresh, including with a cached catalog, while preserving the current selection.
- Windows commands naming `opencode.exe` or `opencode.cmd` use the same installation order as bare `opencode`. Doctor reports the selected OpenCode path and preserves failures from installed executables instead of calling them missing; startup errors include launch failures and early exit details. Windows canonical PATH aliases retain their case spelling. Blocking Doctor checks keep repair or trust-refusal advice, and first-line failure details have no surrounding whitespace.
- Opening Configuration refreshes model queries without removing active pickers from their cache. Manual model refresh can cancel a pending discovery read and recover without reloading the browser; reads started during reload cannot overwrite the refreshed catalog. While manual refresh runs, status and pickers keep showing loading. If it fails, ordinary discovery resumes for each catalog scope that has not loaded, without repeating the reload. OpenCode v2 catalog reads wait for provider activation before reading providers and models, including after reload. This gives delayed providers time to appear even when other models are already available. Empty catalogs return after activation; existing deadlines and cancellation still apply. Only another manual refresh disables the button. The refresh icon is teal at its existing size and location, and model searches show the number of models in the selected catalog scope.
- Regression tests control continuation and autosave timing, wait for subprocess readiness, load startup before timed recovery cases, give independent Manual QA scenarios their own test budgets, exclude test files from browser dependency scans, and assert expected parser warnings. Catalog tests use pending fetches to verify activation, deadlines, and cancellation; council stop-confirmation tests establish prompt startup before advancing the deadline; subprocess tests verify the two-second kill-escalation timer, picker accessibility checks inspect owned option groups, conflict-reload tests wait for content returned by the server, and rewind-warning tests wait for editing to become available.
- Model reads allow 30 seconds in the browser and share a 25-second backend deadline; manual reload allows 60 seconds in the browser and shares a 55-second deadline across safety checks, protocol detection, reload, and catalog refetch. Timeouts use `OPENCODE_DISCOVERY_TIMEOUT`; the first timeout gets one automatic retry even after startup retries, while a second timeout is not retried. Quick startup failures keep their existing eight-retry budget. Reload failures report `reloadState`: a retry repeats the reload POST only when it was not started, and an acknowledged reload retries the catalog GET. An unconfirmed reload failure stops immediately unless it timed out; that timeout gets one catalog GET recovery attempt. Recovered models can remain cached, but the unconfirmed reload still fails and shows an error toast. Configured v1 providers load directly from `/config/providers`; only explicit full-catalog requests use `/provider`, with fallback limited to HTTP 404. Live health checks report connectivity, version, and authentication without loading a catalog, while the health API retains its `models: []` field. Refresh cancels both catalog-query scopes, preserves cached lists on busy responses, and shows rejected refreshes in an error toast. The temporary reload query is removed after success, failure, or cancellation, so a general dashboard refresh cannot repeat its POST. Model pickers distinguish timeouts and retain other error details; caller cancellations and unrelated HTTP failures are not retried.
- Static-analysis configuration declares the repository's ES module format while retaining its existing analyzers and rule thresholds.
- CI downloads verify artifact digests before extracting ZIPs with Python's standard library, removing deprecated Buffer warnings from the download action. Extraction rejects destinations outside the workspace or runner temporary directory, checkout-controlled destination symlinks, Windows alternate data-stream names, and unsafe archive paths.
- The CI port-probe success test scans for an available port instead of assuming its released fixture port stays reserved during parallel tests.
- Release metadata validation tests give each malformed response its own deadline, so process startup time cannot exhaust a timeout shared across all cases.
- Published-install OpenCode probes close each HTTP connection so the final survival check cannot reuse a stale readiness socket. Windows PowerShell children rebuild their standard module paths, keeping Scoop's dependency hash verification available when the driver runs under PowerShell 7. The installed CLI retains the user's original environment.
- Product commands, process-identity checks, folder opening, diagnostics and installers remove incompatible PowerShell 7 module paths only when launching Windows PowerShell. PowerShell 7 and other programs retain their environments; hash verification, archive extraction and CIM process checks remain available through intermediate Node processes.
- Windows published-install checks run under PowerShell so Git's dependency installer can replace its DLLs without Git Bash holding them open. CLI startup captures output in private files and keeps the launcher's real exit status, with a three-minute deadline separate from the health wait, so the CLI can finish its own readiness and failure cleanup. A timed-out launcher receives identity-guarded process-tree cleanup before the driver reports failure. Failed installers and starts retain redacted output and logs, and OpenCode probe errors include server diagnostics. Weekly checks and channel repairs use current CI while release-time checks use the release's workflow. Every leg runs from the workflow's immutable commit; manual repair and reproduction runs select their workflow ref without changing a released package or tag or moving code into another ref's cache security scope.
- A LoopTroop that was killed can leave its own OpenCode running, holding the port with a password only it knew, and `looptroop start` refuses to run alongside it. `looptroop stop` now ends that server before it clears the record, including after it had to kill a daemon that would not shut down, whose kill does not reach OpenCode's own process group. It keeps the record, and exits with an error, while that server or anything it started is still running, or when its identity cannot be confirmed; it used to clear the record and leave the server running. An OpenCode that exited while processes it started still run in its process group keeps its record too: `stop` names them instead of signalling a group it can no longer prove is LoopTroop's, and `start` and `doctor` refuse the record until they are gone. `looptroop doctor` reports the leftover and says to run `looptroop stop`, including when its identity cannot be confirmed (stop it yourself first) and in mock mode. It also fails for the other records a start refuses (a daemon that exited before it finished shutting down, and LoopTroop's own OpenCode recorded without a pid) and for a LoopTroop that is alive but not answering, which a start will not run beside. Its port check counts that daemon's port as LoopTroop's own instead of telling you to stop another process.
- `looptroop doctor` no longer promises that `looptroop start` will launch OpenCode when the address accepts connections but never answers, which makes that start fail, and no longer fails a server that is still starting up and answers with a 5xx error, which a start waits for. It gives OpenCode the same per-request deadlines a start does, so a v1 server that is slow to answer is no longer failed by doctor and accepted by the start.
- `looptroop doctor` could show `node v24.19.0 (latest 22.23.3)`. It read the `latest` tag of npm's `node` package, which follows whatever was published last, even an older line's security release. It now reads nodejs.org's release list and shows the newest release of the Node major line you run.
- Error messages no longer tell you to run `opencode serve` yourself: LoopTroop could never sign in to a server started that way, because OpenCode v2 gives each one its own random password. When OpenCode is not reachable, the model setup screen, ticket errors and the OpenCode upgrade messages say to restart LoopTroop (`looptroop restart`), which starts OpenCode again. When OpenCode is running but refuses LoopTroop, the setup screen, the model picker, ticket errors and `doctor` say so, tell you whether LoopTroop had no password to send or sent a wrong one, and point at `OPENCODE_PASSWORD`. That is decided by what was actually sent, not by an environment variable LoopTroop fills in itself. The setup screen shows the same advice as the model picker, including the variables a v1 server reads, and a ticket error no longer says the refusal twice. A v1 server that refused LoopTroop used to be reported as connected with no models. A server you pointed LoopTroop at that it cannot use comes with the setting to change, and an `opencode` binary refused for where it is installed comes with the option to reinstall OpenCode as yourself.
- The daemon record names the OpenCode by the start identity read when it was launched, read again only while LoopTroop still holds the running child. It used to read it when the record was written, which could pick up another process if OpenCode had exited and its pid had been reused, and `stop` could then signal that process. The first record also describes the OpenCode running once the daemon is up, not one that crashed while it was starting.
- An `opencode` in `~/.opencode/bin` was refused when its folder was writable by its group, even when you owned the folder and the binary. Ubuntu and Fedora give every user a private group and a `002` umask, so the folders the OpenCode installer creates are always group-writable there, and LoopTroop could neither start OpenCode nor pass `doctor`. Permission bits now count only when the binary belongs to another account: the case where root unpacks an official release archive and the binary keeps the build machine's owner (uid 1001). An `opencode` owned by you or by root gets the same ownership check as `git`, `gh` and `npm`, which also means its permission bits are not checked at all, as for those tools.
- npm registry verification allows roughly 30 minutes for publish-time scanning, with a 15-second timeout per polling metadata read, a polling deadline, and a 40-minute job timeout. Container tagging and repair jobs include the shared executable resolver in their sparse checkouts, so Docker commands can start without loading application dependencies. Chocolatey packages include the copyright notice from LICENSE in their nuspec metadata.
- Container repair reads npm's object and one-item array metadata, so the current stable image receives its authorized `latest` and series tags while older releases retain their existing safeguards. Release recovery also unwraps npm field responses before comparing published integrity and dist-tags, so completed releases are recognized correctly. Invalid or ambiguous response shapes stop publication.
- Daemon readiness tests prepare the real schema and process-identity fixtures before timing startup. UI tests synchronize custom events and focus changes with React updates to avoid `act` warnings.
